title: Senegal Hosts Africa's First Olympics — and a Teen Designed the Mascot
summary:
For the first time in history, an Olympic Games will be held in Africa. From October 31 to November 13, Senegal will welcome about 2,700 young athletes, all ages 17 and under, for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.

The competition will spread across three locations: Dakar, Diamniadio, and Saly. Athletes will compete in a wide variety of sports, including skateboarding, cycling, and baseball — a mix that shows how the Youth Games blend traditional events with newer, faster ones.

But the star of the show might not be an athlete. It's Ayo the Lion, the official mascot. Ayo was designed by Ndeye Mariama Diop, a 16-year-old from Senegal. Her lion wears a tingandé, a traditional Senegalese hat made from banana leaves. Ndeye's design was chosen from nearly 500 student entries.

"I was inspired by all the cultures of Senegal," Ndeye told Olympics.com when her design was chosen.

That's a lot of pressure for a teenager — and a lot of pride, too. Her mascot will appear on signs, shirts, and screens around the world, greeting fans at every venue in Dakar, Diamniadio, and Saly.

Think about what that means. The Youth Olympic Games are a stepping stone for young athletes, many of whom will one day compete at the senior Olympics. For Senegal, hosting is a chance to show the world its culture, its hospitality, and its creativity. And for one 16-year-old student, it's a chance to leave a mark that will last long after the closing ceremony.

So keep an eye out. When the Games open in Senegal, a lion in a leafy hat will be right there, welcoming the planet. Not bad for a student art project.
why_it_matters: Where big events are held decides who gets to see themselves in them: an Olympics on African soil gives a whole continent's children a reason to imagine competing. It also shows how countries use hosting to reshape their global image — and how much that costs.

background_read: Senegal is a country on the west coast of Africa whose capital, Dakar, is one of the three places hosting these Games. No African city has ever hosted the main Summer or Winter Olympics, so this is a first for the whole continent.
The Youth Olympic Games are a smaller, newer version of the Olympics for teenage athletes, first held in Singapore in 2010 and then in Nanjing, China and Buenos Aires, Argentina.
Dakar was actually chosen well in advance to host the 2022 edition, but the event was pushed back to 2026 because of the COVID-19 pandemic and unfinished building work.
Senegal is known for 'teranga', a Wolof word for hospitality that many Senegalese describe as the heart of their culture.

Mascots are usually chosen to show something local — Paris 2024, for example, used a Phrygian cap — and Ndeye Mariama Diop (the Senegalese student whose lion design won) followed that tradition with a tingandé hat.

perspectives.description: Hosting lets Senegal show the world its culture, creativity and hospitality, and gives young African athletes a rare chance to compete on a global stage near home. Ndeye's winning design turns one student's artwork into a national symbol seen at every venue.

Hosting is expensive: cities often spend heavily on stadiums, roads and hotels, and critics warn that money could be needed for schools or hospitals. The COVID-19 delay also raised doubts about whether the plans could be delivered on time and used afterwards.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — a test run for the continent
perspectives.description: The Olympics have gone to Europe, the Americas and Asia for more than a century, never to Africa. Because the Youth Games are smaller and cheaper, they are often treated as a trial: stage them well and a future bid for the main Games looks stronger.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — what lasts after the ceremony
perspectives.description: The real test comes after the closing ceremony: whether the venues keep being used, whether Senegalese sport grows, and whether this opens the door to more major events in Africa. For Ndeye, the question is what a 16-year-old does with a global platform.
